preamble: Voicing of [s] to [z] is one of the most common consonant changes. It occurs between vowels or other voiced sounds, as in Western Romance and Old English, before voiced obstruents through regressive assimilation, as in Russian, and in unstressed environments, as with Verner's law in Proto-Germanic. In many languages it is allophonic; in others it became phonemic once the conditioning was lost.

examples.note: Intervocalic voicing of single /s/ in Western Romance.
Northern varieties voice single intervocalic /s/, whereas central-southern Italian keeps [s].
Verner's law: *s became *z when the preceding syllable was unaccented; the *z later rhotacized, giving English were (< *wēzun) beside was.
The fricatives /f θ s/ had voiced allophones [v ð z] between voiced sounds after a stressed syllable; s spelled both [s] and [z].
Regressive voicing assimilation: a voiceless obstruent becomes voiced before a voiced obstruent.

context: Between voiced sounds and before voiced obstruents
allophones_note: /s/ surfaces as [z] between voiced sounds (Old English, northern Italian) or before voiced obstruents (Russian), and [s] is kept elsewhere. In Portuguese and Proto-Germanic the voicing became phonemic.
